title: Repeated DNA Sequences
description: Brute force to optimized: hashing full 10 character strings versus a rolling 20 bit integer encoding.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement
Given a string s made only of the letters A, C, G, and T, return every 10 letter long substring that occurs more than once in s.

blocks.caption: A rolling 20-bit encoding lets each 10-letter window be compared as one small integer

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["Only 4 possible characters (A, C, G, T)","A small, fixed alphabet: each character fits in just 2 bits"],["A fixed-length window (10 characters) slides across the string","Rolling encoding over a sliding window, updating in O(1) per step"],["Need to detect repeated windows efficiently","Hash map keyed by a compact integer encoding instead of the raw substring"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem
Given a string s made only of the letters A, C, G, and T, return every 10 letter long substring that occurs more than once in s.

blocks.title: Analogy: Spotting Repeated Genetic Fragments
blocks.text: Like scanning a long strand of DNA, written using only 4 possible letters, for any exact 10 letter fragment that shows up more than once somewhere along the strand.

blocks.caption: Find every 10 letter window built from A, C, G, T that repeats somewhere else in the string

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: s = "AAAAACCCCCAAAAACCCCCCAAAAAGGGTTT"

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["\"AAAAACCCCC\" appears starting at more than one position","a repeated sequence","The same 10-letter window shows up again later in the string, at a different starting index"],["\"CCCCCAAAAA\" also appears starting at more than one position","another repeated sequence","This window also recurs elsewhere, independently of the first one"],["Answer","[\"AAAAACCCCC\", \"CCCCCAAAAA\"]","Only windows seen more than once are reported; windows seen exactly once are ignored"]]}

blocks.text: Example: s = "AAAAAAAAAAAAA"

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["\"AAAAAAAAAA\" (10 A characters) appears at multiple overlapping starting positions","a single distinct repeated sequence","Even though many overlapping windows are identical, the same 10-character string is only reported once"],["Answer","[\"AAAAAAAAAA\"]","Deduplication happens naturally, since the result only lists distinct sequences, not every occurrence"]]}

blocks.text: Edge case: s shorter than 10 characters
If the string has fewer than 10 characters, no 10 letter window can even be formed, so the answer is an empty list.
5. How Should We Think?
Before jumping straight to a hash map of raw substrings, notice what makes this particular string special: it is built from only 4 distinct letters, not the full alphabet.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A hash map keyed by the actual 10-character substring works correctly, but hashing and comparing full strings at every one of the roughly n positions is real, avoidable work.

Observation 2: Since there are only 4 possible letters, each letter can be represented with exactly 2 bits (00, 01, 10, 11), because 2 bits can distinguish exactly 4 values.

Observation 3: A 10-character window therefore fits entirely inside 20 bits, a single small integer, instead of a 10-character string object.

Observation 4: Moving the window forward by one character does not require rebuilding the encoding from scratch: shifting the old encoding left by 2 bits, masking off anything beyond 20 bits, and OR-ing in the new character's 2-bit code produces the new window's encoding directly from the old one.

Whenever a string problem restricts the alphabet to a small, fixed set of characters, think about packing each character into a few bits and rolling that encoding across the window instead of hashing substrings directly.

This turns an O(n) algorithm with a heavy per-position constant factor, string hashing, into an O(n) algorithm with a light one, integer arithmetic, without changing the overall number of positions visited.
6. Brute Force Solution
For every window of exactly 10 characters, extract it as a string and count how many times each distinct 10 character string appears using a hash map keyed by the string itself.
Step by step algorithm

items: For every starting position where a 10 character window fits, extract that substring.
Count how many times each distinct substring is seen using a hash map.
Return every substring whose count is more than 1.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The loop runs from i = 0 up to n - 10 inclusive (range(n - 9) in Python), exactly the number of positions where a full 10-character window still fits inside the string.
counts.get(window, 0) + 1 / getOrDefault(window, 0) + 1 safely increments a count that may not exist yet, without a separate existence check.
The final filter for count greater than 1 is applied only after every window in the string has been counted, since a window's true total count is only known once the entire string has been scanned.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Every 10 character window is directly counted, so every genuinely repeated sequence is correctly found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), but with a real constant factor cost for hashing and comparing full 10 character strings at every position.
Space: O(n), for the map of full string keys.

Limitation: since each character can only ever be one of 4 possible letters, hashing and storing full 10 character strings is wasteful when each 10 character window could instead be packed into a single small integer.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force already makes exactly one pass over the string, so the number of windows examined cannot be reduced, every window must be looked at once. What can change is the cost paid per window. Extracting and hashing a fresh 10-character string at every position repeats work: 9 of the 10 characters in each window were already part of the previous window. If each character is represented as 2 bits instead of a full character, the previous window's 20-bit encoding can be reused directly: shift it left to make room, mask to keep only the lowest 20 bits, and OR in the 2 bits for the one new character entering the window. The one character that falls off the back of the window is automatically discarded, since it no longer fits inside the 20-bit mask. This turns a full rehash at every position into 3 cheap integer operations.

Encode each of the 4 possible letters as a 2 bit code, so any 10 character window fits entirely into a 20 bit integer. Instead of extracting a new substring at every position, maintain this integer encoding as a rolling value: shift it left by 2 bits, mask it down to the lowest 20 bits, and OR in the new character's 2 bit code, dropping the previous encoding's oldest character automatically. Use a hash map keyed by this integer instead of by string, which is faster to hash and compare.
9. Optimized Solution
Roll a 20 bit integer encoding forward one character at a time, using it as the hash map key instead of a full string.
Dry run for the first few characters of s = "AAAAACCCCCAAAAACCCCCCAAAAAGGGTTT"

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Encode A as 00, C as 01","each character maps to 2 bits","4 letters need only 2 bits, since 2 bits can distinguish exactly 4 values"],["Build the first 10 character window's encoding directly","a single 20 bit integer represents \"AAAAACCCCC\"","10 characters times 2 bits each packs exactly into 20 bits"],["Roll forward one character: shift left 2, mask to 20 bits, OR in the next character's code","the encoding for the next window, without rebuilding from scratch","The mask discards the oldest character's bits once they fall outside the 20-bit window, so the encoding always reflects exactly the current window"]]}

blocks.caption: Optimized: roll a 20 bit integer encoding forward instead of rehashing full 10 character strings

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass with constant work per character.
Space: O(n), for the map of integer encodings, though each key is now a small integer instead of a 10 character string.
Why This Works

Because the mask keeps only the lowest 20 bits, shifting left by 2 and OR-ing in a new 2-bit code both adds the newest character and automatically drops the character that is no longer part of the current 10-character window, so the encoding at any moment corresponds to exactly one specific window, with no ambiguity between different windows.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Bit range","Represents"],"rows":[["Bits 18-19 (most significant)","The oldest character still inside the current window"],["Bits 0-1 (least significant)","The newest character just added to the window"],["Every value from 0 to 2^20 minus 1","One unique combination of 10 characters from the 4-letter alphabet"]]}

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: The first 9 characters are encoded once before the main loop, building a partial 20-bit value covering everything except the last character of the very first window.
Inside the main loop, each new character s[i] contributes its own 2-bit code through encoding << 2 | code[s[i]], immediately followed by masking with & mask to discard any bits beyond position 19.

counts[encoding] is incremented every time a window's encoding is seen, and a substring is only added to the result the moment its count first reaches exactly 2, so it is reported once even if it recurs many more times afterward.

s[i - 9:i + 1] / s.substring(i - 9, i + 1) / s.substr(i - 9, 10) reconstructs the actual 10-character substring for the result, since the integer encoding itself is only used internally for fast comparison.

blocks.text: 10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

Encoding a fixed size window over a small alphabet as a rolling integer, instead of repeatedly hashing full substrings, is a recurring bit manipulation trick whenever the underlying alphabet is small enough to fit a few bits per character.
Common mistakes

items: Forgetting to mask the rolling encoding down to exactly 20 bits after each shift: without the mask, stale higher bits from characters long past the current window silently corrupt the encoding, making two genuinely identical windows compare as different.

Adding a substring to the result more than once: checking for count greater than 1 on every occurrence after the second would append the same string repeatedly, which is why the check must be for the count equaling exactly 2, the one moment it first becomes a repeat.

Assuming this rolling-encoding trick is safe for any alphabet size or window length without rechecking the bit width: a wider alphabet or a longer window can silently overflow the integer type used for the encoding.

blocks.text: Interview tips

items: Mention explicitly why 2 bits per character is enough here (there are only 4 possible letters, and 2 bits can represent exactly 4 distinct values), since recognizing the fit between alphabet size and bits used is the core insight.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "String problem, but the alphabet is tiny, just a handful of distinct characters" points toward packing each character into a fixed number of bits and rolling that encoding across a sliding window, instead of hashing raw substrings.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: What if the window length were variable instead of fixed at 10? A rolling encoding still works, but the mask width must change with the window length, and techniques like polynomial rolling hashes generalize better to arbitrary lengths.

What if the alphabet had more than 4 letters, say 26 for the full alphabet? More bits per character are needed, 5 bits comfortably covers 26 letters, so the encoding no longer fits as tightly, and true string hashing may become more practical again.
How would you return the actual starting positions of each repeat, not just the sequences themselves? Store a list of indices per encoding in the map instead of just a running count.

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Same rolling-window bit-packing idea as Rabin-Karp style rolling hashes, just using exact bit-packing instead of a modular hash function, since the alphabet size here is small enough to pack exactly.
Same "small alphabet means few bits per symbol" insight used in problems like counting distinct characters with a bitmask, or comparing text windows for equality in O(1) after preprocessing.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n) time with a real constant factor for string hashing, O(n) space for string keys.
Optimized (rolling 20 bit encoding): O(n) time, O(n) space, with smaller and faster integer keys.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: Rolling bitmask encoding of a fixed-size window over a small alphabet
Core Idea: Pack each of the 4 possible characters into 2 bits so a 10-character window fits in a 20-bit integer, then roll it forward in O(1) per step
Time: O(n)
Space: O(n) for the map of encodings, the same asymptotic space as the brute force
Most Important Observation: A small, fixed alphabet lets a fixed-length window be represented as one small integer instead of a string, making comparisons and hashing far cheaper
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: 4 letters, 2 bits each, roll the window like a bitmask odometer
